# [A]{.k-a2} — Annotated {#annotated}

::: {.tada-key}
**Annotation** is adding comments **within each code file**, denoted with `#` in
R and Python, or embedding code within an **RMarkdown or Quarto** document
alongside descriptive text. It improves both a reader's ability to *understand*
your archived code (transparency) and their ability to *run* it (functionality
and reproducibility).
:::

Annotation, like Documentation, corresponds to the FAIR principle of Reusable —
the TADA paper states that it does the same job "but rather than describing the
code 'externally', provides clear commenting within each coding script." It is
the letter most often skipped, and it is also much less work done while writing
than reconstructed afterwards.

## Annotate chunks, not lines {#annotated-chunks}

The recommendation is explicit: **annotate code chunks rather than every line of
code.** Line-by-line annotation is possible, but denoting and describing the
relevant chunks in sufficient detail is usually more helpful for tracking what
the code does and what it produces.

A good chunk comment answers three questions:

1. **What** is this chunk doing? *"Run a Poisson generalised linear model…"*
2. **Why** is it needed? *"…to analyse caterpillar abundance varying with
   habitat…"*
3. **Where** does its output appear? *"Numeric results shown in Caterpillar
   Abundance section"*, or *"Figure 5A"*

The third question is **signposting**, and it is the part people leave out. It
is what lets a reader, a data editor or a reviewer connect a number in your
results section to the lines of code that produced it.

:::: {.tada-compare}
::: {.tada-before}
Before

```r
m1 <- glm(n ~ habitat + year, family = poisson, data = dat)
summary(m1)
plot(dat$habitat, dat$n)
```

Nothing tells a reader what is being run, why it is being run, or what it
produces. There is no signposting at all.
:::

::: {.tada-after}
After

```r
##### Caterpillar abundance model #####
# Poisson GLM of caterpillar counts against habitat type, controlling
# for year, to test H1 (abundance differs between woodland types).
# Produces the coefficients reported in Table 2 and the numbers quoted
# in Results, "Caterpillar abundance".
m1 <- glm(n ~ habitat + year, family = poisson, data = dat)
summary(m1)

##### Figure 3A #####
# Raw counts by habitat, plotted as the left panel of Figure 3.
plot(dat$habitat, dat$n)
```
:::
::::

## Collapsible sections {#annotated-sections}

Certain comment markers create **collapsible sections** in the editor, which
increases readability and helps structure a file. This is most useful in long
scripts.

- **`#####`** in RStudio
- **`#%%`** in Python

```r
##### 1. Load and clean data #####
# ...

##### 2. Fit models #####
# ...

##### 3. Figures #####
# ...
```

In RStudio these appear in the document outline, so a reader can navigate a
600-line script from a sidebar instead of scrolling.

## Literate alternatives {#annotated-literate}

Rather than commenting a plain script, you can **embed the code within a
document alongside descriptive text**. The TADA guidelines list this as an
equally valid route to being annotated.

::: {.tabset}

### RMarkdown / Quarto {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Prose and code chunks sit in one file, with the output rendered inline. The
narrative *is* the annotation, and the link between a paragraph of explanation
and the code that follows it is unambiguous.

````{verbatim, lang="markdown"}
## Caterpillar abundance

We fitted a Poisson GLM of counts against habitat type, controlling for
year, to test whether abundance differs between woodland types. These
coefficients are reported in Table 2.

```{r abundance-model}
m1 <- glm(n ~ habitat + year, family = poisson, data = dat)
summary(m1)
```
````

The [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) highlight a further advantage: presenting
everything in one self-contained Markdown or Quarto document is **very helpful
for data editors and future readers**, because it makes the link between the
code, the data and the resulting outputs explicit.

A rendered `.html` or `.pdf` of your Quarto document is a useful *addition* to
the archive, but archive the `.qmd` or `.Rmd` source as well. A rendered PDF on
its own fails [Transferable](#transferable).

### Jupyter Notebook {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Notebooks, and JupyterLab, present code in chunks with descriptive text and
inline output, and are listed in TADA as an alternative route to annotated code.

Two cautions when archiving a notebook (wiki guidance):

- **Restart and run all before you archive.** A notebook whose cells were run
  out of order records a state that nobody can reproduce.
- **Notebooks store output in the file.** That is useful for readers, but it
  means the archived `.ipynb` can be large and awkward to diff. Consider
  archiving both the notebook and a plain `.py` export.

### Plain scripts {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A well-commented `.R` or `.py` file is perfectly adequate, and for many analyses
it is the clearest option. The requirements are the same:

- logical chunks, marked with `#####` or `#%%`
- a comment on each chunk giving what it does, why it is needed and where the
  output appears
- object names that a reader can follow

If the analysis is long, split it across numbered scripts (`01_`, `02_`, `03_`)
and describe the order in the [README](#documented-readme).

:::

## Readability {#annotated-readability}

Annotation works best on code that is already legible. The code review paper
identifies four practices that make code reviewable, and they are set out in
[Writing reviewable code](#review-reviewable): calling packages explicitly by
namespace, using relative file paths, removing redundant packages, and writing
code with clear subheadings, intuitive comments and interpretable object names.

Tooling can enforce a consistent style. **`styler`** (Müller & Walthert 2020)
reformats R code to a standard style in one command, and **`pycodestyle`**
(Rocholl 2022) checks Python code against PEP 8, with `black` or `autopep8` to
do the reformatting. Supported styles include Google and tidyverse in R, and
PEP 8 in Python.

::: {.tada-note}
Style is not the same as annotation. A perfectly formatted script with no
comments still fails the Annotated test. Comments and signposting matter more
than layout.
:::

## Annotating as you go {#annotated-asyougo}

The SORTEE guidelines make the point plainly. Annotating code as you produce it,
not only with section descriptions but also with information about how the code
runs and what output it produces, is **far easier than going back and annotating
at the end of the study**. The same applies to the README: create it at the
start and update it as files are added.

The gain is not only in effort saved. Annotation written months after the fact is
reconstructed from memory, and is more likely to describe what you intended the
code to do than what it actually does.

## Checklist {#annotated-checklist}

- [ ] Code is broken into logical, labelled chunks
- [ ] Each chunk states what it does
- [ ] Each chunk states why it is needed
- [ ] Chunks that produce results signpost the manuscript location (figure, table, section)
- [ ] Collapsible section markers (`#####` / `#%%`) are used in long scripts
- [ ] Object names are interpretable by someone who did not write the code
- [ ] Packages are called explicitly by namespace where it aids clarity
- [ ] Unused `library()` / `import` calls have been removed
- [ ] If using a notebook: it has been restarted and run top to bottom before archiving
- [ ] If using Quarto or RMarkdown: the **source** file is archived, not only the rendered output
